what_it_does: RowHammer is an attack where an adversary repeatedly reads rows of memory cells near a target row, causing electrical disturbance that flips bits in the target row and corrupts or leaks data. JEDEC (the industry standards body for memory) introduced a new DDR5 memory feature called PRAC (Per-Row Activation Counting) that lets each memory module count how many times each row has been accessed and signal the memory controller to perform a preventive refresh of neighboring rows before a bit flip can occur. The problem is that existing implementations of PRAC-based defenses are either insecure under the actual JEDEC specification, or require the memory controller to have perfect knowledge of which rows are most at-risk — information it cannot easily obtain. QPRAC solves this by building a priority queue inside the memory controller: rows are ranked by how many times they have been activated, so the most-endangered rows are always refreshed first. Two additional techniques piggyback extra protective refreshes onto normally scheduled memory operations, keeping the performance overhead small.
